case_name: Walter Buchanan murder of Darrel Odhiambo

scenes.text: At 7:12 in the morning, a 66-year-old man called emergency services. He said he'd woken up and found his wife cold beside him.
He said he tried CPR. He said he didn't know what happened.
What he left out — to the 911 operator, to the paramedics — was the fight.
And the fight wasn't about her cheating on him. It was about a text message that proved he was cheating on her.
Walter Buchanan was 66 years old, a chartered surveyor with what the court would later call "a successful professional working life."
Darrel Odhiambo was 37, originally from Kenya, a mother to a young son.
They met in 2015, while Buchanan was on holiday in Thailand. They married two years later, in 2017.
By February 2023, they'd been married six years, living together in an upmarket flat near Hamilton racecourse, in South Lanarkshire, Scotland.
On paper, it read like a comfortable life — a respected local professional, a well-off address, a marriage six years in.
Friends and neighbours would later say the marriage had turned volatile. Darrel had confided in people close to her about the abuse.
After her death, investigators found a text message on her phone — sent by Buchanan. It read: "I hope you die you black b****."
Nobody outside that relationship had any way of knowing exactly how bad it already was — until the night everything came apart.
On February 18th, 2023, Darrel found a text message on her husband's phone. It read: "I guess you are having fun in Bothwell without your wife, cheater."
Bothwell is a town just a few miles from their own home — whatever Buchanan had been doing, he hadn't even gone far to do it.
She confronted him with it. This wasn't Darrel being accused of cheating — it was Darrel catching him.
By Buchanan's own account, given at trial, Darrel lunged at him. They fell. She was dragged across the floor.
Later, when she followed him into the bedroom, still calling him a cheater, he grabbed her by both wrists and pushed her onto the bed.
Buchanan admitted to what happened next. He placed his hand over her face. He grabbed her by the neck, with one hand, for what he said was only a matter of seconds.
He said he pushed her face into a pillow. He said she rolled onto her side afterward.
The post-mortem told a different story than "a matter of seconds." Darrel died of manual strangulation and smothering — significant compression to the neck, a brain injury, bruising, a fractured rib.
Four distinct injuries, from a man who described his own hands on her as brief and almost incidental.
At 7:12 the next morning, Buchanan called for help. He told the operator he'd simply found her unresponsive. He told paramedics the same thing.
He never mentioned the fight. Not to the 911 operator. Not to the paramedics who arrived and tried to save a woman who was already gone.
Buchanan denied murder. He went to trial at the High Court in Glasgow, and stood by his version: that this was a struggle that went wrong, not a killing.
It took over a year after Darrel's death before Buchanan was even remanded into custody to await that trial — and nearly two years, total, before a jury ever heard the case at all.
The prosecution's case rested on a simple, damning contrast — a man who claimed innocence to a jury, after already lying by omission to the people who'd tried to save his wife's life.
Lord Cubie, the judge, would later put it plainly: Buchanan's own incomplete account to emergency responders was itself evidence — proof, in the court's own words, of "a consciousness of guilt."
The trial ran eight days. Buchanan's own account of the struggle was put in front of the jury in his own words — lunging, dragging, wrists, a pillow, seconds.
It didn't match what the post-mortem found on Darrel's body.
And it didn't match how Buchanan had actually behaved that morning — a man who'd had hours to call for help immediately, and chose instead to wait, then leave out exactly what had happened.
On January 22nd, 2025, the jury reached its verdict: guilty of murder.
Sentencing came on April 2nd, 2025, at the High Court in Edinburgh.
Lord Cubie sentenced Walter Buchanan to life in prison, with a punishment part of 15 years before he can even be considered for parole.

Moira Orr, the homicide lead for Scotland's prosecution service, spoke for the record: "Darrel Odhiambo was a loving mother, daughter, sister and friend, who had the right to be safe in her relationship and home."
It's a simple sentence. It's also exactly the thing Buchanan took from her.
Buchanan had one minor prior conviction before this. A "successful professional working life," as the court put it — nothing that marked him out, on paper, as capable of this.
Darrel's mother and sisters spoke of their grief and frustration in the aftermath of the trial — grief for the woman they'd lost, frustration at how long it had taken to get here.
News of the case reached Kenya, too — carried by outlets there as the story of a Kenyan woman killed thousands of miles from home, by the man she'd left everything to marry.
Her son is growing up without his mother, because his stepfather couldn't stand being caught.
Not caught in a lie about her. Caught in a lie of his own — the one written in a text message he never should have sent, to someone who wasn't his wife.
He had the chance, that morning, to tell the truth the first time he picked up the phone. If he had — would anything about what happened to Darrel have been different?
Or was the lie always going to be the last thing he chose to protect?
